methodology: Real R2 (staging bucket), real functions from app.routers.downloads/app.services.serve_time_video (compose_serve_time_dispatched, _download_cache_key, r2_head_object_global, download_from_r2_global, upload_file_to_r2_global). No DB/FastAPI/auth -- isolates the exact cache mechanism's I/O+compose cost. Source fixture: synthetic 60s 810x1440@30fps h264 clip (2.4MB), uploaded to R2 scratch to make the MISS path's R2 fetch leg representative (an earlier run using a bare local file without the R2 fetch leg understated MISS -- superseded, not included below). MISS = real R2 fetch of source + compose_serve_time_dispatched + real R2 upload to cache key. HIT = real R2 HEAD + real R2 download of the cached composed file. Both paths share the per-request _stamp_download cost (not measured here since it runs unconditionally on both hit and miss, per the download_metadata.py NOTE ON CACHING contract -- it does not differentiate hit vs miss).
env: APP_ENV=staging, real reel-ballers-users R2 bucket, run from host (not container -- containers lack real R2/Modal per T4180)
caveats: Compose here ran LOCAL ffmpeg (0.265s), not a real Modal network round-trip -- modal_enabled() resolved to local in this invocation; a Modal-dispatched compose would widen the MISS/HIT gap further since it adds R2 scratch upload + dispatch + cold start + download-back on top of the local compose time this measurement captured.

Synthetic 2.4MB fixture is far smaller than a typical multi-minute highlight (tens of MB); both MISS's fetch+upload legs and HIT's head+download legs would scale up roughly proportionally with real file size, but MISS additionally pays compose+upload that HIT entirely skips -- so the absolute time saved (not just the ratio) should grow, not shrink, for real-sized reels.
This does not measure the FIRST-ever download/share of a highlight (the task's own documented residual-latency case) -- by definition a first request is always a MISS.
